lessons.title: Engagement Patterns in Physical Activity and Sport
lessons.description: Current participation trends and the factors that affect engagement across different social groups.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Engagement Patterns?

Engagement patterns describe who participates in physical activity, how often, and in which activities. They vary significantly across different social groups — not because of differences in ability, but because of the social, cultural, economic and practical factors that shape people’s lives. Understanding why participation differs between groups is central to this topic, because the goal of sport policy is to remove barriers and make physical activity genuinely accessible to everyone.

Current participation trends in the UK are tracked by several respected bodies. Sport England publishes the Active Lives survey, which measures participation across age groups, sports and regions. National Governing Bodies (NGBs) collect data specific to their own sport. The Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) oversees national sport strategy and funding. Together these sources give a picture of who is active and where the gaps remain.

Factors Affecting Participation: Social and Cultural

Several social and cultural factors shape engagement patterns. Gender remains a significant variable: women and girls historically face barriers including sexism, stereotyping and lower media coverage of women’s sport, which limits the visibility of female role models. When Beth Mead scored a hat-trick at the 2022 UEFA Women’s Euros, grassroots girls’ football registrations rose sharply — evidence of how role models translate directly into participation.

Ethnicity and religion/culture add further dimensions. Race-based discrimination creates hostile environments that deter participation in clubs and competitions. Cultural norms within some communities restrict female participation in mixed-sex sport or in activities where uniform requirements conflict with modesty expectations. Religious observance — prayer schedules, fasting periods, festival commitments — can create scheduling conflicts with training and competition. Coaches and clubs that show flexibility around these factors can significantly improve engagement for these groups.

Age shapes participation across the life course. Young people participate at higher rates when PE is compulsory and sport is embedded in school life. Participation often drops sharply after leaving school as competing demands of work and family life reduce available leisure time. Older adults face different barriers: declining physical capacity, fewer social networks, fewer accessible activities, and negative stereotypes about what older people can or should do. Accessible provision — walking football, seated yoga, aqua aerobics — is critical for sustaining engagement in older age groups.

Key Fact

Sport England, National Governing Bodies (NGBs) and the DCMS are the three main sources of participation data in the UK. Social and cultural barriers include sexism and stereotyping (gender), discrimination (ethnicity), cultural and religious scheduling conflicts, and age-related stereotyping and declining provision for older adults.

Factors Affecting Participation: Economic and Practical

Socio-economic factors cut across all groups. Cost and disposable income determine whether a family can afford club memberships, specialist equipment, coaching fees and travel to competitions. Young people from lower-income households are significantly less likely to participate in organised sport. Free or subsidised community sport programmes are therefore critical to equitable access.

Time and work commitments are a persistent barrier for adults. Working patterns, shift work, childcare and caring responsibilities all compete with leisure time. Women are disproportionately affected by caring commitments, which partly explains lower participation rates among adult women in formal sport. Family influence cuts both ways: children whose parents participate in sport are significantly more likely to be active themselves, because parents model behaviour and provide the practical support — transport, fees, kit — that enables participation.

Education shapes early exposure: schools that offer a diverse range of activities build habits of participation that often persist into adulthood. Opportunity and access depend on whether suitable facilities exist locally. Environment and climate affect participation in outdoor activities — rural communities may lack indoor facilities, while urban areas may have limited green space for field sports. Media coverage and visible role models matter enormously: when a sport receives little media attention, potential participants never encounter it as a realistic option. Role models from under-represented groups signal that a sport is “for people like me.”

People with physical or intellectual disabilities historically face some of the most significant barriers to sport participation. Physical barriers include inaccessible facilities (steps rather than ramps, no hoist equipment in pools), lack of adapted equipment and absence of disability-specific sessions. Attitudinal barriers are often harder to address: negative stereotypes assume that disabled people are not interested in or capable of competitive sport. Dame Sarah Storey’s 17 Paralympic gold medals and the growth of wheelchair basketball as a spectator sport challenge these assumptions directly. Where governing bodies and leisure centres invest in adaptive provision — boccia, sitting volleyball, goalball, deaf-friendly coaching — participation among disabled groups rises.

Strategies to Improve Participation

The OCR specification identifies three strategies that bodies such as Sport England and NGBs use to improve participation. Promotion involves raising awareness of physical activity opportunities through advertising, campaigns and role model endorsements. Sport England’s “This Girl Can” campaign used promotion to target women who felt sport was not for them, directly challenging stereotypes. Provision means creating and maintaining physical activity opportunities: building accessible facilities, funding community sport programmes, training coaches and creating adapted sessions for under-represented groups. Access refers to removing practical barriers that prevent people from taking part even when opportunities exist — subsidising membership costs, providing transport, scheduling sessions at times that suit working parents, and ensuring facilities are physically accessible.

Key Fact

Three strategies to improve participation: Promotion (raising awareness and challenging stereotypes through campaigns and role models), Provision (creating opportunities, facilities and adapted sessions), and Access (removing practical barriers such as cost, transport and scheduling). All three are needed together for sustained change.

Students sometimes treat engagement barriers as isolated, single-cause problems. In reality, a person’s engagement is typically shaped by several factors simultaneously. A woman from a lower-income ethnic minority background in a rural area with caring responsibilities faces overlapping economic (cost), cultural (stereotyping, discrimination), geographical (access) and practical (time) barriers at once. A strong extended-response answer will recognise this overlap — and note that strategies must address multiple factors together, not in isolation, to produce lasting improvements in engagement patterns.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On a 4 marks — Interpret Data question about engagement patterns, you must do three things: quote a specific figure from the data, make a comparison, and explain what it shows in a sporting context. Simply reading a number earns nothing — the mark scheme rewards the inference. For example: “Disabled students participate at 22% compared to 68% for male students — a gap of 46 percentage points — suggesting significant access or inclusion barriers for this group at this school.” On a 6 marks — Analyse question, avoid listing factors one by one. Instead, develop each point: name the factor, explain the mechanism, give a specific sporting example. A common error is addressing only one group. The spec requires knowledge of multiple social groups — aim to discuss at least two contrasting groups with specific barriers for each.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Engagement patterns are tracked by Sport England, National Governing Bodies (NGBs) and the DCMS. They reveal persistent inequalities across social groups — caused by social, cultural, economic and practical barriers, not differences in ability.
  • Key barriers include: sexism and limited media coverage (gender), discrimination and cultural/religious conflicts (ethnicity/religion), age-related stereotyping and declining provision (age), inaccessible facilities and attitudinal bias (disability), and cost/time/access limitations (socio-economic).
  • Three OCR-named strategies to improve participation: promotion (awareness and role models), provision (facilities and sessions), access (removing practical barriers). All three must work together for sustained improvement.

lessons.title: Commercialisation, Sponsorship and the Media
lessons.description: The golden triangle of sport and the positive and negative impacts of media and sponsorship.
lessons.content_html:
What is Commercialisation?

Commercialisation is the process by which sport is bought and sold as a product. Sport generates enormous revenue through ticket sales, television rights, merchandise and sponsorship deals. As sport became a global entertainment industry, businesses saw it as a powerful vehicle for reaching audiences and building brand recognition. The result is that money now flows into sport from commercial partners at every level — from grassroots clubs to elite international events.

The Golden Triangle

The relationship between sport, sponsorship and the media is described as the golden triangle. Each corner supports and benefits the other two. Sport needs funding; sponsors need audiences; the media needs content to attract viewers and readers. These three parties are mutually dependent. For example, a major football tournament attracts millions of television viewers, so broadcasters pay billions for the rights to show it. Those viewing figures attract sponsors who pay to have their logos seen. The tournament organisation uses that income to fund prize money and infrastructure, raising the quality of competition, attracting more viewers — and the cycle continues.

Key Fact

The golden triangle links sport, sponsorship and the media in a mutually reinforcing relationship. Sport provides content, the media provides an audience, and sponsors provide money in return for visibility with that audience.

Types of Media

OCR identifies four types of media that influence the commercialisation of sport. Social media has transformed sport by allowing direct communication between athletes and fans, instant highlights sharing and viral marketing — an athlete’s post can reach tens of millions of followers within minutes. Athletes like Dina Asher-Smith and Marcus Rashford use their platforms to build personal brands that attract sponsors independently of their governing bodies. The internet allows fans to access highlights, statistics and analysis at any time, breaking the dependence on scheduled broadcast. Television (TV/visual) provides the largest audiences and the highest revenue; live broadcasting rights to major leagues and tournaments are worth hundreds of millions of pounds. Newspapers and magazines provide in-depth analysis and reporting, though print circulation has declined as digital media has grown.

Before social media, fans learned about athletes almost exclusively through television and newspapers, and an athlete’s public image was tightly controlled by PR teams. Social media disrupted this entirely: athletes now communicate directly with fans, comment on social issues and build personal brands independently. This gives athletes greater power but also greater exposure to criticism. A single post can generate positive or negative coverage almost instantaneously, and a viral moment can be more commercially valuable than a traditional advertising campaign.

Types of Sponsorship

Sponsorship takes three main forms. Financial sponsorship involves a company paying an athlete, team or event directly in return for advertising exposure — for instance, a bank sponsoring a tennis player so its logo appears on their clothing. Clothing and equipment sponsorship means a manufacturer provides kit, footwear or specialist equipment. A sprinter may wear a named brand’s spikes and appear in their advertising. Facility sponsorship involves a company paying for the naming rights or upkeep of a venue. In every case, the sponsor’s goal is to increase brand awareness and sales by associating with a popular or prestigious sporting figure or event.

Positive and Negative Effects of the Media on Commercialisation

The media’s influence on commercialisation has both positive and negative effects. On the positive side, extensive broadcast coverage raises the profile of sport, attracting more viewers, which in turn attracts sponsors and generates income that can be reinvested into the sport. Television coverage of the Women’s Super League has grown significantly in recent years, drawing new sponsors and raising participation at grassroots level. Social media enables sports to reach global audiences at minimal cost, increasing their commercial appeal. On the negative side, less commercially attractive sports receive little or no media coverage, limiting their ability to attract sponsors and leaving them under-resourced. Media can also create an intrusive spotlight on athletes’ private lives, adding to psychological pressure. Kick-off times may be changed to suit overseas television audiences, prioritising commercial interests over the experience of home fans.

Key Fact

Commercialisation benefits performers through financial security and increased profile, but creates pressures including media scrutiny, the expectation to compete when injured, and obligations to commercial partners that can conflict with athlete welfare.

Positive and Negative Effects of Sponsorship on Commercialisation

For individual performers and sports, sponsorship has both enabling and constraining effects. Positively: sponsorship income allows elite athletes to train full-time without financial worry, access cutting-edge equipment and coaching, and reach new audiences through their sponsors’ marketing channels. Broadcast revenue funds leagues, which fund academies, which develop future talent. For sport itself, commercial investment has raised standards at elite level through investment in facilities, coaching and performance science. Negatively: commercial priorities can distort sport. Sponsors may withdraw from an athlete or sport after a controversy, removing critical funding suddenly. The pressure to perform for commercial partners can be intense: athletes may feel obligated to compete when injured or to act as brand ambassadors in ways that feel inauthentic. Rising ticket prices driven by commercial revenue can price out traditional fans. Less commercially viable sports may be marginalised entirely.

Many students argue that commercial money is purely positive for sport. This is too one-sided. While funding raises standards, commercial interests can prioritise profit over sporting values. Some competitions have been rescheduled to times inconvenient for home fans purely to suit international television markets. Grassroots sports with smaller audiences often receive little or no commercial support. A strong extended-response answer must acknowledge both positive and negative effects on multiple groups: performers, sport itself, audiences and sponsors.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On a 6 marks — Analyse question about commercialisation, list-style answers score poorly. Each point should follow a three-step structure: state the impact, link it to how it affects a specific group (performer, sport, audience, sponsor), then give a plausible sporting example. On an 8 marks — Evaluate question, you must discuss both positive and negative impacts. A common error is writing only positives or only negatives — OCR’s levels-based mark scheme explicitly rewards a balanced argument. Use a ‘For X… However Y…’ structure and anchor each side to a sporting context. For example: “Sponsorship income allows elite athletes to train full-time [positive]. However, commercial pressure can force athletes to compete while injured to meet contractual obligations [negative].”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The golden triangle links sport, sponsorship and the media in a mutually reinforcing cycle — each corner depends on and supports the other two.
  • OCR identifies four media types: social media, the internet, television and newspapers/magazines. Each has distinct commercial reach and influence on sport.
  • Commercialisation has positive impacts (financial security for performers, higher standards, wider audiences) and negative impacts (pressure on athletes, distorted scheduling, exclusion of less commercial sports and lower-income fans).

lessons.title: Ethics in Sport: Sportsmanship, Gamesmanship and Deviance
lessons.description: The value of sportsmanship and the reasons performers turn to gamesmanship or deviance.
lessons.content_html:
How Performers Are Expected to Behave

Sport is governed not only by written rules but by unwritten codes of conduct that define how athletes are expected to treat opponents, officials and the spirit of competition itself. These codes range from formal customs to cultural expectations, and they are often tested most severely when the pressure to win is at its greatest. Understanding the difference between behaviour that upholds sporting values and behaviour that exploits or undermines them is central to sport’s identity as more than a simple contest of skill.

Etiquette

Etiquette refers to the unwritten rules of conduct in sport — customs that participants are expected to follow even though they are not written into the official rule book. In tennis, it is considered etiquette to acknowledge a lucky net cord with a gesture to your opponent. In golf, players are expected to repair divots, rake bunkers and maintain silence when others are playing. In cricket, a fielding side traditionally applauds a departing batsman who has played well. None of these behaviours are compulsory under the laws of the game, but failing to observe them draws social disapproval and signals a disrespect for the sport’s traditions.

Sportsmanship

Sportsmanship describes behaviour that embodies fair play, respect and generosity in competition. A sportsmanlike act might include a footballer kicking the ball out of play when an opponent is injured so they can receive treatment, despite there being no rule requiring it. It includes shaking hands with opponents after a match, accepting officials’ decisions without complaint, and refusing to take advantage of an opponent’s misfortune. Sportsmanship is widely seen as a moral standard to which all competitors should aspire, regardless of the stakes.

Key Fact

Etiquette is the unwritten code of conduct in a sport (customs and traditions). Sportsmanship is the attitude and behaviour of fair play, respect and generosity towards opponents and officials. Both go beyond the written rules and reflect the spirit of competition.

Gamesmanship

Gamesmanship sits at the opposite end of the conduct spectrum from sportsmanship. It involves using strategies that are technically within the rules but deliberately break their spirit to gain an unfair advantage. Examples include: a tennis player bouncing the ball an excessive number of times before serving in order to disrupt an opponent’s concentration; a rugby player deliberately slowing play by lying on the wrong side of a ruck for as long as the referee will allow; or a batsman calling for a new bat purely to break the bowling side’s rhythm when momentum is building. Gamesmanship is legal but widely considered unsporting.

Gamesmanship is distinguishable from outright cheating because it stays within the formal rules. Cheating — such as deliberately handling the ball in football or falsifying a time in athletics — breaks the written rules and can result in disqualification. Gamesmanship breaks the spirit but not the letter of the law. However, the boundary is contested. At what point does prolonged time-wasting become a cynical act that undermines the sport? At what point does verbal distraction (sledging in cricket) cross from psychological contest into intimidation? These questions generate rich material for extended-response questions because they have no simple answers.

Deviance in Sport

Deviance in sport refers to behaviour that goes against the accepted norms and values of sporting competition. Unlike gamesmanship (which stays within the rules) and etiquette breaches (which are a matter of custom), deviance typically involves a more serious violation of sporting or social norms. Examples of deviant behaviour include: using performance-enhancing drugs; deliberately injuring an opponent; match-fixing; and persistent verbal abuse of officials.

OCR identifies three main reasons why performers engage in deviant behaviour. First, the desire to gain an unfair advantage: in a highly competitive environment where the margins between success and failure are tiny, some performers are willing to break the rules if they believe it will increase their chances of winning. Second, peer pressure: within certain sporting cultures, deviant practices (such as aggressive fouling or using banned substances) may be normalised to the point where an individual feels pressured to conform in order to be accepted by teammates or coaches. Third, a win-at-all-costs culture: when winning is prioritised above all other values — by athletes, coaches, clubs or the media — the ethical boundaries that constrain behaviour are gradually eroded. Financial incentives at elite level can amplify this: the prize money, sponsorship and status attached to winning creates intense pressure to succeed at any cost.

Key Fact

Three reasons for deviance in sport: (1) to gain an unfair advantage over opponents; (2) peer pressure within a sporting culture that normalises unethical behaviour; (3) a win-at-all-costs culture driven by financial rewards, media pressure and the status attached to success.

Students often use etiquette and sportsmanship interchangeably, and confuse both with deviance. They are distinct concepts. Etiquette is sport-specific customs (how you are expected to behave in that particular sport). Sportsmanship is a broader moral attitude about how you treat opponents and the spirit of competition across all sport. Deviance is behaviour that violates norms and values — it is a more serious concept than a lapse of etiquette or even an act of gamesmanship. In a 6-mark question, use all three terms accurately: describe the etiquette of a specific sport (e.g. kicking the ball out in football when an opponent is injured), describe sportsmanship as a general value (e.g. shaking hands after the match), and distinguish deviance as a normative violation — not just poor manners, but a rejection of sporting values altogether.

The Value of Sportsmanship

These concepts matter beyond individual events. Sport’s social and cultural value rests partly on its reputation as an arena in which effort, skill and fair competition determine outcomes. When gamesmanship becomes widespread, public trust in sport erodes. When deviance is normalised, sport loses its role as a model of positive values for young participants. Research into youth sport suggests that the conduct of elite athletes influences the attitudes of young people who aspire to perform at a high level. Athletes who model sportsmanship — acknowledging good play by opponents, respecting officials, competing without cynicism — provide a more powerful form of influence than those who win by any means necessary.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 3 marks — Describe question on etiquette, students often give one-word answers like “etiquette means respect.” To earn 3 marks, describe the concept fully (what it is), give a specific sporting example, and explain why it matters. For a 6 marks — Analyse question, avoid listing definitions. Instead, analyse how sportsmanship, gamesmanship and deviance each shape the experience of sport for different groups — performers, officials and young participants. A critical OCR-specific distinction: deviance is on the OCR spec as a separate term from gamesmanship. Be clear that deviance violates sporting norms and values (it goes further than simply bending the rules), and always give the three OCR reasons (unfair advantage, peer pressure, win-at-all-costs culture) when asked to explain why performers behave deviantly.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Etiquette is the unwritten code of conduct in a sport (customs and traditions); sportsmanship is the broader moral attitude of fair play, respect and generosity towards opponents and officials.
  • Gamesmanship exploits loopholes within the rules to gain a psychological or tactical advantage — it is within the rules but against their spirit, and widely considered unsporting.
  • Deviance is behaviour that violates the norms and values of sport. OCR identifies three reasons: gaining unfair advantage, peer pressure, and win-at-all-costs culture driven by financial reward and media pressure.

lessons.title: Drugs in Sport
lessons.description: Why performers use drugs, the named PED categories and the impact of drug use on sport and performers.
lessons.content_html:
Performance-Enhancing Drugs in Sport

Performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs) are substances that athletes take to improve their physical or psychological output in training or competition. Most PEDs are prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) and the governing bodies of individual sports. The use of prohibited substances is considered cheating because it undermines the principle of fair competition and often poses serious health risks to the performer. Despite this, doping remains a persistent problem across numerous sports at elite level.

Why Performers Use Drugs

OCR requires students to understand the reasons why sports performers use performance-enhancing drugs. The most fundamental driver is the desire to gain a competitive advantage: in high-level sport, where the difference between winning and losing can be fractions of a second or tiny increments in strength or endurance, a substance that delivers even a marginal performance improvement may be the difference between a gold medal and obscurity. Linked to this is the pressure of financial reward: elite sport is a career, and success brings sponsorship, prize money and media contracts. Where the incentive to win is enormous, the temptation to use any available means is correspondingly strong.

A second cluster of reasons involves cultural and peer pressure. If a performer believes that their competitors are using prohibited substances — creating what they perceive as an uneven playing field — they may feel compelled to use them simply to compete on the same terms. Within some sporting environments, doping may be tacitly encouraged by coaches, management or team culture, making it difficult for an individual to refuse. A win-at-all-costs culture, reinforced by media attention and commercial pressure, can erode the ethical barriers that would otherwise constrain behaviour. Finally, some performers use drugs not to win but simply to recover from injury more quickly, to train harder, or to manage the physical demands of a very high-performance training schedule.

Key Fact

Performers use PEDs to gain a competitive advantage, because of financial incentives, due to peer pressure or a win-at-all-costs culture, or to recover more quickly and train harder. OCR requires knowledge of exactly three PED categories: anabolic steroids, beta blockers and stimulants.

Key Fact

WADA publishes an annually updated prohibited list covering hundreds of substances across every sport. Athletes bear strict liability — a positive test result leads to a ban regardless of whether the performer knew they had taken the substance.

Anabolic Steroids

Anabolic steroids are synthetic hormones that accelerate the development of muscle mass and reduce recovery time between training sessions. They are most commonly associated with power-based sports — such as weightlifting, shot put, sprinting or rugby — where muscle mass is a direct determinant of performance. By allowing performers to train harder and recover faster, anabolic steroids provide a substantial competitive advantage. Side effects include liver damage, cardiovascular disease, hormonal disruption (including effects on secondary sexual characteristics), and in adolescent users, premature closure of growth plates, which can permanently reduce adult height.

Beta Blockers

Beta blockers reduce heart rate, lower muscle tension and decrease blood pressure by blocking the effects of adrenaline. In sports requiring extreme precision — such as archery, shooting or snooker — a reduced heart rate and steadier hand provides a direct performance advantage, as even a small tremor can affect accuracy. Beta blockers are prohibited by WADA in these specific sports because they provide an unfair advantage. Side effects include nausea, weakness and potentially dangerous cardiac problems. They should only be used under medical prescription.

Stimulants

Stimulants are substances that increase alertness, reduce the sensation of fatigue and heighten aggression and competitiveness. They can improve reaction time and allow a performer to sustain high-intensity effort for longer. Sports such as sprint cycling or combat sports, where aggression and alertness are direct performance assets, have seen stimulant misuse. Side effects include elevated heart rate, anxiety, insomnia and in severe cases cardiac arrest. Stimulants are banned in competition by most governing bodies.

Anabolic steroids benefit power and strength athletes (e.g. a shot-putter who needs greater muscle mass and faster recovery). Beta blockers benefit precision performers (e.g. an archer whose accuracy is affected by a raised heart rate under competition pressure). Stimulants benefit high-speed or combat sport athletes (e.g. a sprint cyclist who needs maximum alertness and aggression over a short burst of effort). Matching the PED to the sport type and explaining the mechanism is the key skill tested in 1-mark Identify and 3-mark Describe questions on this topic.

Impact of Drug Use on Performers

The impact of PED use on individual performers is both physical and social. On the physical side, all three PED categories carry significant health risks: liver damage and cardiovascular disease (anabolic steroids), cardiac problems and weakness (beta blockers), and cardiac arrest or insomnia (stimulants). Beyond health, performers who are caught face bans from competition, fines, and the loss of medals and records. Reputational damage can be permanent — a performer’s entire career may be overshadowed by a doping conviction, affecting future coaching roles, sponsorship opportunities and public standing long after retirement.

Impact of Drug Use on Sport Itself

For sport as a whole, high-profile doping scandals damage credibility: if spectators suspect that results are determined by chemistry rather than talent and effort, they lose trust in the sport. This can reduce attendance, television audiences and sponsorship revenue — feeding back through the golden triangle to reduce the resources available to all performers, clean or otherwise. Sport’s value as a positive social model — promoting health, effort and fair competition — is also undermined when doping becomes associated with a discipline. Governing bodies and anti-doping agencies must invest heavily in testing programmes, which diverts resources from development and participation.

Some performers argue that if everyone is doping, using PEDs simply restores a level playing field. This reasoning should be challenged. First, not all athletes dope — those who refuse are placed at a systematic disadvantage. Second, access to the safest and most effective doping protocols depends on resources, meaning wealthier athletes and nations dope more effectively than poorer ones — an inequality within an inequality. Third, normalising PED use accelerates health risks for all performers by creating a race to ever-higher levels of doping. A strong 8-mark answer will recognise this argument, acknowledge why it holds superficial appeal, and then dismantle it with these counter-points.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On a 1 mark — Identify question about a PED, name the category precisely: “anabolic steroids”, “beta blockers” or “stimulants”. For a 3 marks — Describe question about a specific PED, give three distinct pieces of information: what the substance does, which type of performer would use it and why, and one side effect. Avoid repeating the same point in different words. On an 8 marks — Evaluate question about whether PED use can be justified, you must present genuine arguments on both sides. A response that only condemns PED use without engaging with the reasons performers give for using them will be capped at the Developing band. Use a ‘For X… However Y…’ structure anchored to a sporting example on each side. Remember: OCR specifies only three PED categories — no credit for blood doping, EPO or narcotic analgesics on this specification.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • OCR requires knowledge of exactly three PED categories: anabolic steroids (muscle growth — power sports), beta blockers (reduced heart rate/tremor — precision sports) and stimulants (alertness/reduced fatigue — sprint/combat sports).
  • Performers use PEDs for competitive advantage, financial reward, peer pressure and win-at-all-costs culture. All three categories carry significant health risks and lead to bans, fines and reputational damage if detected.
  • Drug use damages sport itself through loss of credibility, reduced spectator trust, falling sponsorship revenue, and diversion of governing body resources into anti-doping programmes.

practice_questions.text: A 17-year-old county-level sprinter is told by a senior teammate that 'everyone uses stimulants to get an edge at the top level' and that testing is rarely carried out at county competitions. practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation presenting genuine arguments on both sides. Uses accurate physiological vocabulary (alertness, reduced fatigue, heart rate, side effects). Challenges the 'everyone does it' reasoning with counter-arguments. Reaches a reasoned, balanced conclusion. Consistent sporting application. Arguments are developed, not just listed.

Acceptable arguments for: stimulants increase alertness and reduce fatigue, directly improving sprint performance (1); may level the perceived playing field if the sprinter believes others are using them (1); low perceived risk of detection at county level reduces fear of sanction (1).
Arguments against: stimulants carry real health risks including elevated heart rate, anxiety and in extreme cases cardiac arrest - especially dangerous in a young person (1); the 'everyone does it' argument is flawed: many competitors do not use PEDs, so use creates an unfair disadvantage for clean athletes, not a level field (1); if detected at any level, consequences include a ban, loss of results and a permanent record that could affect future opportunities (1); drug use violates the principles of fair competition and the spirit of sport, causing reputational harm even if not detected (1); the teammate's claim is ethically inappropriate - peer pressure of this kind is one of the key reasons young performers are drawn into deviant behaviour, and the sprinter has the right to refuse (1).
Conclusion: stimulant use is both ethically wrong and practically risky; the short-term performance gain is outweighed by health risks, the unreliability of the 'level playing field' argument, and the long-term consequences for the sprinter's career and integrity.

lessons.title: Violence in Sport
lessons.description: The reasons for player violence and how violence affects performers, officials and sport.
lessons.content_html:
Violence in Sport

Player violence in sport refers to aggressive behaviour by performers that goes beyond the accepted rules and physical contact of their sport. Some contact sports — rugby, ice hockey, boxing — involve physical aggression that is governed and regulated by the rules. Player violence, however, refers to acts that break those rules: late and dangerous tackles, deliberate elbowing, stamping, head-butting, or verbal threats and abuse directed at opponents or officials. It is distinct from the sanctioned physicality that is part of many sports, and it is the illegitimate crossing of that line that is the focus of this topic.

Frustration

One of the most commonly cited causes of player violence is frustration. When a performer’s goals are persistently blocked — by opponents who consistently foul, by a run of bad fortune, by their own errors or by what they perceive as poor officiating decisions — emotional tension builds. For some performers, this tension discharges as verbal or physical aggression towards opponents or officials. In football, for example, a striker who has been repeatedly fouled and denied a clear penalty may eventually retaliate physically against the player they perceive as responsible. This link between frustration and aggression is well documented in sport psychology: the key insight for OCR is that frustration alone rarely produces violence — it combines with other factors, such as rivalry or alcohol, to lower a performer’s inhibitions.

Rivalry and the Importance of the Contest

High-stakes rivalry is a consistent context for player violence. When two teams or performers have a long competitive history, or when a match carries exceptional importance — a cup final, a relegation decider, a historic derby — the emotional stakes are elevated. Performers who would behave within acceptable limits in a routine fixture may be more likely to commit a violent act under the pressure of a high-stakes encounter. In ice hockey, intense rivalry between clubs has historically produced confrontations that go beyond the regulated physical contact of the sport. In cricket, the intensity of an Ashes Test has been the context for episodes of verbal and physical aggression that would not occur in a county match between the same players.

Key Fact

Five key causes of player violence: frustration (blocked goals cause tension that discharges as aggression), rivalry/importance of contest (high emotional stakes lower inhibitions), alcohol and drugs (impair judgement and increase impulsivity), officiating decisions (real or perceived injustice triggers retaliation), win-at-all-costs culture (intimidation seen as a legitimate performance tool).

Key Fact

National governing bodies (NGBs) can issue bans, fines and mandatory education programmes in response to player violence. Repeated incidents in a sport may prompt the NGB to introduce rule changes — for example, introducing sin bins or citing commissioners — to deter violent conduct and protect the sport’s reputation.

Alcohol and Drugs

The influence of alcohol and drugs on player violence operates primarily by reducing impulse control and lowering the psychological inhibitions that normally prevent aggressive behaviour. A performer who has consumed alcohol before or during a sporting event is more likely to react violently to a provocation that a sober individual would absorb without incident. Alcohol is also a significant factor in violence among spectators at events, which can in turn escalate tensions on the field of play. In rugby, concerns about the culture of post-match drinking within teams have occasionally been linked to incidents of violence both on and immediately after the pitch.

Officiating Decisions

Perceived injustice stemming from officiating decisions is a well-documented trigger for player violence. When a performer believes they have been the victim of an incorrect decision — a penalty awarded against them unfairly, a red card given for a challenge they consider legitimate, or repeated decisions that seem to favour the opposition — the perceived injustice compounds their frustration and can provoke an aggressive response. Verbal abuse of officials is the most common form this takes, but physical confrontation does occur. In football, scenes where players crowd around a referee following a controversial decision reflect the intensity of this reaction, even when physical violence does not follow.

In some sporting environments, a win-at-all-costs culture actively encourages intimidation as a performance strategy. Physical aggression that technically exceeds the rules may be tolerated or even coached as a means of unsettling opponents, disrupting their rhythm or forcing them into errors. This is distinct from gamesmanship (which stays within the rules) — deliberate physical intimidation that risks injuring opponents represents a form of deviance that reflects a culture where winning outweighs the ethical boundaries of sport. When this culture is embedded in a team or club, individual players face peer pressure to participate in or at least not challenge the behaviour, normalising violence over time.

The Impact of Player Violence on Sport and Performers

Player violence has significant negative consequences for all involved. For performers who commit violent acts, the immediate consequence is disciplinary action — red cards, sin bins, match bans and in severe cases criminal charges. The long-term consequences can include reputational damage that reduces sponsorship opportunities and career longevity. Performers on the receiving end of violence face injury risks, psychological distress and the possibility of long-term physical harm. For officials, violence directed at them — whether physical or verbal — is both personally distressing and damaging to the integrity of their role. The threat of abuse deters qualified officials from continuing in sport, creating a shortage of referees and umpires at all levels. For sport itself, repeated episodes of violence damage the sport’s public image, reduce its appeal to families and casual spectators, make it harder to attract sponsors, and undermine its role as a positive model for young participants.

Students sometimes confuse this topic with spectator violence or hooliganism, which is an AQA focus. OCR’s specification places its emphasis on player violence — the behaviour of the performers themselves during competition. The spec states that learners should “know and understand the reasons for player violence” and “give practical examples of violence in sport.” While spectator behaviour may be mentioned as contextual background (e.g. crowd atmosphere raising tensions), your exam answers should keep the focus firmly on what players do and why, not on crowd disorder.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On a 2 marks — State Two question asking for causes of player violence, make sure your two answers are genuinely distinct — “frustration” and “anger” describe the same thing and score only 1 mark. OCR accepts: frustration, rivalry, alcohol/drugs, officiating decisions, win-at-all-costs culture, retaliation or intimidation as a strategy. On a 6 marks — Analyse question, avoid listing causes one by one without development. Each cause should be developed: name it, explain the mechanism by which it leads to violence, and give a specific sporting example. A common error is focusing only on one sport (usually football) — include examples from at least two different sports to show breadth. Keep the focus on player violence, not spectator behaviour, as OCR’s specification specifically requires this focus.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Player violence is aggressive behaviour by performers that exceeds the rules of a sport. OCR’s focus is on player violence, not spectator hooliganism. Key causes: frustration, rivalry/importance of the contest, alcohol and drugs, disputed officiating decisions, and win-at-all-costs culture.
  • Impacts on performers include disciplinary bans, injury risk, reputational damage and reduced sponsorship. Impacts on officials include personal distress and a deterrent effect on referee recruitment.
  • Impacts on sport include reputational damage, reduced spectator appeal, loss of sponsorship and the undermining of sport’s role as a positive social model for young people.

lessons.title: Characteristics and Classification of Skill
lessons.description: Motor skills, the characteristics of skilful movement and the difficulty and environmental skill continua.
lessons.content_html:
What is a Motor Skill?

In physical education, a motor skill is a movement that has been deliberately learned and can be reproduced with accuracy and control. Unlike reflexes or instinctive reactions, motor skills are developed through practice. A novice footballer attempting a lofted pass for the first time is displaying very little skill; a county-level midfielder delivering a precise long ball under pressure has refined that movement through thousands of repetitions until it is consistent, efficient and goal-directed. The key idea is that motor skills are learned — they improve with practice and can be broken down, coached and refined.

Five Characteristics of Skilful Movement

OCR specifies five characteristics that distinguish a skilful movement from a clumsy or untrained one. When you watch an elite performer, all five are visible simultaneously.

Efficiency — a skilful movement uses only the muscles and energy required to complete the task. There is no wasted effort, no unnecessary tension and no redundant sub-movements. A seasoned marathon runner carries their arms low and relaxed; an elite swimmer pulls with a high elbow to maximise propulsion while minimising drag. Beginners waste energy through excess tension; skilled performers conserve it through economy of movement.

Pre-determined — a skilful movement has a clear intended outcome before it begins. The performer knows what they want to achieve and has a plan. A netball shooter stepping up for a penalty pass has already visualised the arc, the release point and the target before the ball leaves their hand. This intention guides the movement pattern from start to finish, rather than the performer discovering the outcome as they go.

Co-ordinated — different body parts work together in the correct sequence to produce the movement. In a javelin throw, the approach run, the crossover step, the hip drive, the shoulder rotation, the elbow extension and the wrist flick all combine in a precisely timed chain. If any link fires too early or too late, the sequence breaks down. Skilled performers produce these multi-limb co-ordinations fluently and automatically.

Fluent — the movement flows smoothly from one phase to the next without jerking, pausing or hesitation. Fluency is the visible sign that the performer has moved beyond the cognitive stage of learning (where each sub-routine is consciously executed) into the autonomous stage (where the movement runs automatically). A beginner swimming breaststroke will pause awkwardly between the pull and the kick; an experienced swimmer blends the phases seamlessly.

Aesthetic — a highly skilful movement is pleasing to watch. Not every sport rewards aesthetics formally (gymnastics and diving award marks for it; sprinting does not), but even in functional sports, observers recognise something visually satisfying about a perfectly struck golf drive, a clean double-leg takedown in wrestling, or a long-range curved shot curling into the top corner. Aesthetic quality is generally a by-product of the other four characteristics: a movement that is efficient, co-ordinated and fluent will tend to look graceful.

Key Fact

The five OCR characteristics of skilful movement are: efficiency (no wasted energy), pre-determined (clear intent before execution), co-ordinated (body parts linked in sequence), fluent (smooth, uninterrupted flow) and aesthetic (pleasing to observe). These apply to all motor skills, not just artistic sports.

The Two Skill Continua

OCR uses two continua to classify skills. A continuum is not a binary label but a spectrum — most skills fall between the two extremes, and the performer must justify the placement rather than simply attach a label. Both continua must be applied when classifying a skill for examination purposes.

Continuum 1: Simple to Complex (Difficulty)

The difficulty continuum runs from simple skills at one end to complex skills at the other. A simple skill demands very little from the performer in terms of decision-making, number of movements to co-ordinate simultaneously, or perceptual processing. Walking in a straight line, performing a standing jump, or rolling a ball along a flat surface are all towards the simple end.

A complex skill, at the other end, involves many sub-routines that must be co-ordinated simultaneously, a wide range of possible responses, and heavy demands on attention. A tennis serve — which requires the ball toss, stance, backswing, contact point and follow-through all to be synchronised — sits towards the complex end. A basketball lay-up sits between the two: it follows a set pattern (making it less complex) but requires simultaneous co-ordination of running, jumping and release angle (making it more demanding than a simple catch). The difficulty continuum is defined by how many decisions and sub-routines the skill involves, not by whether the environment is changing.

Continuum 2: Open to Closed (Environmental)

The environmental continuum describes how predictable the environment is while the skill is being performed. This is one of the most commonly confused continua in GCSE PE — open and closed refer to the environment, not to whether the skill is difficult. An open skill takes place in an unstable environment. A football pass under pressure from a defender is an open skill because the positions of teammates, defenders and the ball change from moment to moment, and the performer must adapt their movement continuously.

In contrast, a closed skill takes place in a stable, predictable environment. A gymnast performing a floor routine executes each element in the same unchanging space; a swimmer diving from the block always enters the same lane. Because the environment is fixed, the movement pattern can be pre-planned and repeated identically each time. The open-to-closed continuum is about environmental predictability, nothing else.

Many students write that a skill is “open because it is difficult” or “closed because it is simple” — this confuses the two continua and will lose marks. A highly complex gymnastics floor routine is a closed skill (environment is predictable and controlled) but sits at the complex end of the difficulty continuum. A simple one-touch pass in football is an open skill (defenders and teammates move unpredictably) but may be a straightforward movement in terms of co-ordination demands. Always base your open/closed answer on whether the environment is changing and unpredictable (open) or stable and predictable (closed). OCR only uses two continua — keep them clearly separate in your answers.

Key Fact

OCR uses only two skill continua: (1) Simple — Complex (difficulty): how many decisions, sub-routines and attentional demands the skill involves. (2) Open — Closed (environmental): how predictable and stable the environment is. Every skill classification answer should address both continua with justification. Most skills sit between the extremes, not at either end.

Worked Example: Classifying a Rugby Lineout Throw

A hooker throwing into a lineout can be placed on both continua. On the simple — complex continuum, the lineout throw sits towards the complex end: the hooker must co-ordinate the grip, run-up, elbow extension and wrist release while simultaneously reading where the jumpers are and which code the team has called. Multiple sub-routines and a range of decision-making demands push it away from the simple end. On the open — closed continuum, it sits towards the open end during match play: opposing players may disrupt the lineout, jumpers' positions change based on opposition movement, and the throw must adapt to a dynamic situation. However, during a training drill with no opposition, the same throw would shift towards the closed end — the environment is now predictable and the movement can be pre-planned.

On any skill classification question, simply writing “it is an open skill” earns no marks. Examiners require the justification: why is the skill open or complex? The justification must reference the correct definition — e.g. “it is an open skill because the environment is unpredictable; the positions of defenders and teammates change continuously so the performer must adapt”. The definition-based justification is what earns the mark, not the label. When placing a skill on the continuum, avoid placing it exactly at one extreme unless you can justify why it could not move any further in either direction — most realistic sport skills sit somewhere between the two poles.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On ‘explain’ and ‘analyse’ questions about skill classification, the most common error is stating a classification without justifying it using the continuum definition. Writing “it is an open skill” alone earns nothing — you must say why (e.g. “it is an open skill because the environment is unpredictable; defenders are repositioning and the performer must adapt continuously”). For an 8-mark evaluate question, always address both continua for each skill scenario, provide a justified placement on each, and apply your answer to a named sporting example. A common error is confusing the two continua — remember: simple/complex is about the number of decisions and sub-routines, while open/closed is about environmental predictability. These are separate dimensions and must be justified separately. On the 5-characteristic question, if asked to ‘describe’ three characteristics, don’t just name them — give a brief sporting example of each to access the full marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The five characteristics of skilful movement are efficiency, pre-determined, co-ordinated, fluent and aesthetic — these distinguish practised, expert performance from untrained movement.
  • OCR uses two skill continua: simple–complex (difficulty — how many decisions and sub-routines are involved) and open–closed (environmental — how predictable the environment is).
  • Always justify your skill classification using the continuum definition, not just the label. Classify every skill on both continua with reasoning.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a closed skill?
A) A basketball player receiving a bounce pass from a teammate during a fast break
B) A gymnast performing a vault on a consistent, controlled run-up
C) A tennis player returning a serve from an opponent
D) A rugby scrum-half passing after receiving a ball from a maul
practice_questions.marks: B) A gymnast performing a vault on a consistent, controlled run-up [1 mark]. The environment is stable and predictable; the movement can be pre-planned and repeated identically. All other options involve unpredictable, changing environments (open skills).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'open skill' in the context of sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the core idea: a skill performed in an unpredictable or changing environment. 1 mark for development: the performer must adapt their movement continuously to respond to changes in the situation (accept: opponents, teammates, or external conditions change and the performer reacts to them). Do not credit definitions that describe open skills as difficult or unstructured.

practice_questions.text: Describe three characteristics of skilful movement, using a sporting example for each.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each characteristic correctly described with a brief sporting example (up to 3 marks). Accept any three of: efficiency — no wasted energy or movement, e.g. an elite swimmer using a high elbow pull to maximise propulsion without excess drag (1); pre-determined — the performer has a clear intended outcome before executing, e.g. a netball shooter visualising the arc before releasing (1); co-ordinated — body parts work in correct sequence, e.g. the approach, hip drive and arm action of a javelin throw combining in a timed chain (1); fluent — movement flows smoothly without pausing, e.g. an experienced breaststroke swimmer blending the pull and kick phases seamlessly (1); aesthetic — the movement is pleasing to observe, e.g. a curved finish shot curling into the top corner (1). Maximum 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: A football coach watches a Year-7 pupil attempt a long pass and notices jerky, hesitant movement with wasted arm tension. Explain how this contrasts with the characteristics of skilful movement shown by an elite midfielder.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for identifying weaknesses in the beginner: movement is not fluent (pausing/jerking between sub-routines) (1); energy is wasted through excess muscle tension, so it lacks efficiency (1). Up to 2 marks for linking to characteristics shown by the elite player: the elite midfielder's movement is fluent — phases blend seamlessly (1); it is efficient — only the required muscles fire in the correct sequence, conserving energy (1). Accept references to co-ordinated or pre-determined with appropriate sporting application.

practice_questions.text: A county athletics coach is classifying the discus throw and the 100-metre hurdles on OCR's two skill continua. Analyse the placement of each event on both continua, justifying your answers.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses both skills on both continua (four placements total) with clear, definition-based justifications. Discus throw — simple/complex: towards the complex end; requires co-ordination of approach, spin, hip drive, arm swing and release angle, multiple sub-routines demanding simultaneous control (1); open/closed: towards the closed end during competition; the circle is a fixed, controlled environment and the performer initiates when ready, with no opposition interfering (1). Hurdles — simple/complex: more complex than a flat sprint, as the athlete must time the take-off, lead leg clearance and trail leg mechanics for each barrier (1); open/closed: towards the closed end; the hurdles are fixed positions, the track is constant, the environment is predictable (1). Strong responses note that both events are towards the closed end of the environmental continuum but differ on the difficulty continuum. Consistent use of continuum terminology and definitions throughout.

Secure: Correctly places both events on at least three of the four continuum positions, with mostly accurate justifications. May be less precise on one placement.

Developing: Places each event on one continuum only, or gives correct labels without justification. Some continuum terminology used.

Emerging: Names the continua without placing either skill; or confuses the two continua definitions.

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old club swimmer competes in both sprint freestyle events and open-water swimming races. Evaluate the view that the two OCR skill continua give a complete and useful picture of how these two activities differ as sporting skills.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A balanced, well-developed evaluation with a range of points on each side, each applied to the swimming scenario, with a clear and justified conclusion. Arguments in support: the two continua do capture key differences — pool sprint freestyle is towards the closed end (predictable lane, no opponents to dodge) but open-water racing sits further open (currents, other competitors' position, turns around buoys vary); the difficulty continuum distinguishes the more complex demands of open-water navigation (multiple environmental stimuli to process) from the more straightforward cyclic arm-pull pattern of pool freestyle; using the continua helps coaches design appropriate training — pool training can be highly repetitive/closed-skill-focused, while open-water prep needs open-skill adaptability drills. Arguments against: two continua cannot fully capture all distinctions between sports; the five characteristics of skilful movement add a dimension the continua miss (e.g. efficiency differences between the two settings); other factors such as fitness level, pacing strategy and tactics are not addressed by skill classification; the placement on a continuum is somewhat subjective and may vary with the specific race conditions. Justified conclusion: the two continua are a useful starting framework for comparing skills but should be used alongside other analytical tools for a complete picture.

Secure: Two or three developed points on each side, mostly applied to the swimming scenario, with a reasonable conclusion.

Developing: Points on both sides but limited development; may focus on one swimmer only; thin sporting application.

Emerging: One-sided or very basic response; little or no sporting application to the scenario.

lessons.title: Goal Setting and SMART Targets
lessons.description: Why we set goals in sport and how the SMART principle is applied to improve performance.
lessons.content_html:
Why Goal Setting Matters in Sport

Elite and recreational athletes alike use goal setting to direct effort and track progress. Without a clearly defined target, training can feel purposeless — athletes may work hard without knowing exactly what they are working towards. OCR identifies three distinct purposes for goal setting: to support exercise and training adherence, to motivate performers, and to improve and optimise performance. These three purposes are closely connected: a well-set goal keeps the athlete coming back to training (adherence), gives them a reason to push harder (motivation), and provides the framework for progressive development (performance improvement).

Goal Setting for Adherence

One of the most significant challenges in sport and physical activity is getting people to stick to training over time. Dropout rates are high, particularly among young people and those new to a sport. Goal setting reduces dropout by giving training a clear direction. When an athlete knows they are working towards a specific target — shaving two seconds off their 400 m personal best, increasing their maximum push-ups from 15 to 25 by the end of term — each session has a purpose. That sense of progress and purpose is a powerful driver of continued participation. Without it, training can feel like pointless repetition.

Goal Setting to Motivate

Goals provide the emotional fuel that drives a performer through demanding sessions. Knowing that a target is within reach — but requires consistent effort — keeps motivation high across a training programme. The target also provides a reference point for measuring effort: if you can see the gap closing between where you are now and where you want to be, each training session feels worthwhile. Kelly Holmes is a well-cited example of an athlete who used goals to maintain intense motivation through years of injury setbacks; her clarity about her Olympic 800 m and 1500 m targets helped sustain commitment through periods when the outcome felt distant.

Goal Setting to Improve Performance

Performance improvement requires structure. A goal provides the benchmark from which progress is measured and the endpoint towards which training is designed. Coaches use goals to plan progressive overload: if a cyclist aims to hold 280 watts for 20 minutes by the end of an eight-week block, each week’s sessions can be calibrated against that target. Without the goal, training lacks direction and improvement tends to plateau. The goal also sharpens the focus of the performer during sessions — they know which aspect of performance they are developing and why.

Key Fact

OCR identifies three purposes of goal setting: (1) to support exercise/training adherence — keeping athletes engaged and returning to training; (2) to motivate performers by giving them a reference point for progress; (3) to improve and optimise performance by providing a structured target for progressive development.

The SMART Principle

A goal is only useful if it is well-constructed. Vague intentions such as “get fitter” or “play better” provide no actionable direction. The SMART framework turns vague intentions into specific, trackable targets. In OCR Physical Education, SMART stands for: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Recorded and Timed. Note carefully that OCR uses “Achievable” and “Recorded” — these are different from other variants of the acronym used by other examination boards.

Breaking Down SMART

Specific: the target must state clearly what is to be achieved. “Get better at swimming” is not specific. “Reduce my 100 m freestyle time from 75 seconds to 70 seconds by the end of the half-term” is specific. A specific goal focuses training effort on exactly the right area and removes confusion about what success looks like.

Measurable: progress must be trackable using objective data. Times, distances, repetition counts, percentage success rates and scores all provide measurable evidence of progress. Without a measurable element, the performer cannot objectively determine whether they are improving or standing still.

Achievable: the goal must be within reach given the performer’s current ability, available training time and circumstances. A target that is too easy provides no motivational challenge. A target that is clearly impossible leads to frustration and demotivation. The ideal SMART target stretches the performer just beyond their current level — demanding real effort but attainable with consistent work. A county-level 400 m runner setting a target of running 44 seconds — a world-class standard — within six weeks would be setting an unachievable goal; targeting a two-second improvement on their current personal best is achievable.

Recorded: the goal must be written down and documented. Recording the goal creates accountability — both the performer and their coach can return to it, check progress and adjust the training plan if needed. An unrecorded goal exists only in memory, where it can be forgotten, altered unconsciously or abandoned without consequence. Recording also makes the goal real: when a young athlete writes down “I will achieve 15 press-ups in a set by the end of this month”, they are making a commitment that can be reviewed and celebrated or revised.

Timed: every SMART goal needs a deadline. “Improve my conversion rate to 60% by the end of the season” has a timed element; “improve my conversion rate eventually” does not. A deadline creates urgency, allows coaches to plan a progressive training schedule and provides a natural review point at which the goal can be evaluated and the next target set.

Different examination boards use slightly different versions of the SMART acronym. OCR’s version is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Recorded, Timed. The critical differences are the A and the R. Some boards use “Accepted” for A (meaning the goal is agreed with the coach) — OCR uses “Achievable” (meaning the goal is within reach). Some boards use “Realistic” for R — OCR uses “Recorded” (meaning the goal is documented). Writing the wrong letters in an OCR exam will cost marks on definition questions. Drill the exact five words: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Recorded, Timed. The A and the R are the exam traps.

Key Fact

OCR’s SMART = Specific (clearly defined), Measurable (trackable with data), Achievable (challenging but realistic), Recorded (written down and monitored), Timed (has a clear deadline). Learn these five exact words — not “Accepted” or “Realistic”, which are used by other boards.

Imagine a 15-year-old club sprinter whose current 100 m personal best is 12.8 seconds. A SMART target might be:

“Reduce my 100 m personal best from 12.8 seconds to 12.4 seconds (specific, measurable) within the next 10 weeks of structured sprint training (timed). An improvement of 0.4 seconds is achievable given my current fitness trajectory and twice-weekly coaching sessions (achievable). This target is written in my training log and reviewed with my coach after each weekly time trial (recorded).”

Every element of SMART is present. The recorded element is demonstrated by the training log entry and the regular coach review. The timed element gives both performer and coach a clear endpoint from which to work back and plan each week’s sessions.

On the 1-mark identify question, remember the three purposes: adherence, motivation, and performance improvement — any one of these earns the mark but the answer must be precise enough to be one of these three concepts.

Key Takeaways

  • Goal setting has three purposes in OCR PE: to support exercise and training adherence, to motivate performers, and to improve and optimise performance.
  • SMART targets must be Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Recorded and Timed — OCR uses ‘Achievable’ and ‘Recorded’, not the variants used by other boards.
  • A recorded goal is one that is written down and tracked over time, creating accountability for both the performer and the coach.
