lessons.title: Mental Preparation Techniques
lessons.description: Imagery, mental rehearsal, selective attention and positive thinking applied to sporting performance.
lessons.content_html:
The Mental Side of Sport

Physical fitness and technical skill are not enough to guarantee peak performance. Elite athletes consistently report that the mental dimension of their preparation is as important as their physical training. Missing a penalty, misjudging a serve at a crucial moment, or freezing under pressure before a major competition — these experiences are not failures of technique alone. They reflect psychological factors that can be trained and managed. OCR identifies four mental preparation techniques that performers use to optimise their psychological readiness: imagery, mental rehearsal, selective attention and positive thinking. Each technique addresses a different aspect of the performer’s mental state, and together they form a practical toolkit for performance preparation.

Imagery

Imagery is the deliberate creation of vivid mental pictures associated with sport. Unlike simply “thinking about” a sport, effective imagery engages multiple senses — the sound of the crowd, the texture of the ball, the sensation of the playing surface underfoot, the feeling of muscles working at full effort. A long-jumper preparing to compete might use imagery to experience, in vivid detail, the feeling of the approach run, the plant foot striking the board, the explosive drive of the hips and the moment of landing. A basketball player might image the sound of the ball swishing through the net.

Imagery works because the brain’s response to a vividly imagined experience shares many of the same neural pathways as the actual experience. Detailed, multi-sensory imaging creates a mental state of readiness that bridges the gap between preparation and competition. Imagery can also be used to manage nerves — a performer who has repeatedly imaged calm, controlled execution in a high-pressure moment is less likely to feel the situation as novel or overwhelming when it arrives. Adam Peaty has described using detailed imagery before major championship heats, imprinting a sense of familiarity onto what would otherwise feel like unique, high-stakes moments.

Mental Rehearsal

Mental rehearsal is the internal simulation of a complete performance or skill sequence, carried out in the mind before physical execution. Where imagery is primarily about creating a sensory experience, mental rehearsal has a more structured, procedural focus: the performer runs through the exact sequence of movements they intend to execute, in correct order, as if previewing the performance from inside their own body.

A diver performing a new list of dives at a national competition would use mental rehearsal to run through each dive in the correct sequence — approach, hurdle step, take-off, tuck position, entry — several times before mounting the board. Research shows that mentally rehearsed movements activate many of the same motor pathways as physically performed movements, effectively providing “practice” that reinforces the movement programme without physical effort or risk. Mental rehearsal is most effective when performed in real time (not rushed), in the first person (from the performer’s own perspective), and always picturing successful execution rather than errors.

Key Fact

Imagery creates a vivid multi-sensory experience of sport, engaging feelings, sounds and visual detail — it prepares the mind for the competitive environment. Mental rehearsal is a structured run-through of the skill sequence itself, rehearsing the exact movement programme before physical execution. Both techniques are used in the period before competition. Both picture success, never failure.

Selective Attention

Selective attention is the skill of directing focus towards the information that matters and filtering out everything else. Competition environments are full of potential distractions: crowd noise, opponents’ behaviour, negative internal thoughts, environmental conditions. A performer who has not trained their attention will find that these distractions invade their focus at precisely the moments when concentration is most critical.

Training selective attention means deliberately practising the ability to lock onto task-relevant cues — the flight of the ball, the position of a defender, the feel of the racket at contact — while choosing to ignore everything else. A tennis player preparing to receive a serve must direct all attention to the server’s ball toss and racket path, blocking out crowd noise, score awareness and anxiety about the point. A sprinter in the blocks must focus on the starting gun and their own movement activation, filtering out lane-side distractions and the presence of rivals. Dina Asher-Smith has spoken about developing a “tunnel vision” process in the call room before major finals, systematically narrowing attention to her own race plan.

Selective attention is developed through repeated practice, cueing routines (where the performer identifies specific cues to focus on) and mental preparation before competition. It is closely linked to both imagery and positive thinking — a performer who has imaged the task clearly and has a positive mental script is better able to focus on task-relevant cues because there is less cognitive space for distractions to fill.

Positive Thinking

Positive thinking involves consciously replacing negative internal dialogue with prepared, constructive thoughts. In sport, negative thinking is extremely common: “I always miss these”, “I’ve never done well in this arena”, “everyone is watching me”. Left unchallenged, negative thoughts reduce confidence, tighten muscles, narrow attention in unhelpful ways and can trigger the self-fulfilling prophecy of poor performance. Positive thinking is the deliberate psychological counterattack.

The technique works by having the performer prepare a set of positive, task-focused mental statements in advance of competition. These statements are not empty slogans but specific, believable reminders that redirect attention towards what the performer can do: “I have trained this kick hundreds of times”, “I trust my technique”, “smooth contact, follow through”. When negative thoughts arise — and in high-pressure moments they will — the performer activates their prepared positive script, interrupting the negative loop and redirecting focus to the execution cues.

Positive thinking does not require ignoring difficulty or pretending a situation is not pressured. It is realistic self-support: acknowledging the importance of the moment while maintaining belief in preparation. A rugby goal kicker who thinks “this kick matters AND I have the skill to execute it” is using positive thinking effectively. A kicker who tells themselves “this is fine, I never miss” when their recent form has been poor is not — that is denial, which collapses under real pressure.

Elite athletes rarely use just one mental preparation technique in isolation. Before a major competition, a gymnast might use mental rehearsal (running through the floor routine in sequence), imagery (experiencing the feel and sound of the hall and the sensation of the tumble run), selective attention (narrowing focus to the floor and the music, filtering out the score and the audience), and positive thinking (“I have trained this routine for six months — my body knows what to do”). Together, the four techniques create a psychological state of readiness in which the performer is fully focused on successful execution. In an exam, you may be asked to explain how one specific technique works or to evaluate the relative usefulness of the four techniques — make sure you can describe the mechanism of each separately before discussing how they combine.

Key Fact

Four OCR mental preparation techniques: (1) Imagery — vivid multi-sensory mental pictures that prepare the mind for competition. (2) Mental rehearsal — a structured run-through of the skill sequence in the mind before physical execution. (3) Selective attention — focusing on task-relevant cues while filtering out distractions. (4) Positive thinking — replacing negative internal dialogue with prepared positive scripts to maintain confidence.

OCR’s sports psychology unit covers the four techniques above and no more in this section. The following topics appear on other examination boards but are NOT assessed by OCR and should not appear in your answers: arousal and the inverted-U theory; information processing models; personality types; aggression types; motivation types; contract to compete. If a question asks you about mental preparation in sport, restrict your answer to imagery, mental rehearsal, selective attention and positive thinking. Adding content from outside the OCR specification will not gain marks and may suggest to the examiner that you are confused about the scope of the course.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On 4-mark explain questions about mental preparation, the most common error is describing a technique without explaining why it works. Writing “the athlete uses imagery to picture themselves succeeding” earns only 1 mark. To earn the full 4, you must also explain the mechanism — “imagery activates similar neural pathways to physical performance, creating a sense of familiarity with the competitive situation and building confidence before the event” — and apply it to the specific scenario in the question. On the 8-mark evaluate question, always ensure you cover all four techniques (or at least three) and that you consider both the benefits and any limitations. OCR’s levels-based mark scheme rewards range, balance and sporting application. A common pitfall is writing only about one technique in depth — that approach will cap your mark in the lower bands. Use a ‘For X... However Y...’ structure for each technique, anchored to a named sporting example.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • OCR identifies four mental preparation techniques: imagery (vivid multi-sensory mental pictures), mental rehearsal (structured internal run-through of the skill sequence), selective attention (filtering out distractions to focus on task cues), and positive thinking (replacing negative thoughts with prepared positive scripts).
  • Mental rehearsal is most effective when performed in real time, first-person and always picturing successful execution — not errors.
  • The four techniques are often used together and reinforce each other; athletes develop them through deliberate practice as a core part of their preparation routine.

practice_questions.text: A club-level gymnast is preparing for her first national competition. Her coach suggests she incorporates all four mental preparation techniques into her warm-up routine. Evaluate how effective each technique could be in helping her perform at her best.

Conclusion: all four techniques contribute and they work best in combination; selective attention and positive thinking are most immediately deployable, while imagery and mental rehearsal require more practice to be fully effective. lessons.title: Types of Guidance in Sport
lessons.description: Visual, verbal, manual and mechanical guidance with their advantages and disadvantages.
lessons.content_html:
Guidance in Sport — The Instruction Side of Coaching

Every sports coach must decide how to help a performer learn or refine a skill. The method chosen is called guidance — it is the instructional side of coaching, distinct from feedback (which evaluates performance after it has happened). OCR requires you to know four types of guidance: visual, verbal, manual and mechanical. For each type, you must understand what it is, its advantages and disadvantages, and when it is most appropriate — particularly whether it suits a beginner or an elite performer. The most effective guidance method depends on the stage of learning, the nature of the skill and any safety considerations.

1. Visual Guidance

Visual guidance is any form of instruction that the performer sees. The most common form is a live demonstration: a coach or skilled model performs the skill, and the learner watches and forms a mental image of the correct movement pattern. Beth Mead demonstrating cutting runs in the penalty area to a group of youth players is visual guidance. Video analysis, tactical diagrams on a whiteboard, and highlighted zones on a pitch are all forms of visual guidance.

Advantages of visual guidance: It provides a complete, whole-skill picture of what correct performance looks like. For beginners, who have no movement pattern stored in memory, seeing the skill demonstrated gives them the mental blueprint they need. Video can be paused, replayed and slowed down for detailed analysis. For elite performers, video analysis can reveal subtle technical faults that verbal description alone would miss — a sprinter watching slow-motion footage of their arm drive can identify asymmetry that was invisible in real time.

Disadvantages of visual guidance: The quality of the demonstration is critical — a poor-quality or inaccurate model confuses rather than clarifies. Beginners may struggle to pick out the key features of a complex demonstration if given no cues about what to focus on. Video analysis requires equipment and is not always practical during a session. A demonstration only shows external form, not the internal feel of the movement.

2. Verbal Guidance

Verbal guidance uses words to instruct. A coach saying “bend your knees on take-off”, calling “watch the ball!” during a rally, or giving tactical instructions before a match are all examples of verbal guidance. Words can convey precise technical information, tactical instructions and corrections quickly. Verbal guidance is time-efficient and can reach an entire group simultaneously.

Advantages of verbal guidance: Fast and efficient — a single precise cue can trigger an adjustment in an experienced performer without interrupting the flow of training. Can be delivered mid-performance (e.g. a rowing coach calling from a launch beside the boat). Highly effective for elite performers who already have a movement pattern stored in long-term memory — a precise cue such as “drive the elbow earlier on the catch” activates and refines an existing programme.

Disadvantages of verbal guidance: Complex movements are difficult to describe in words alone. A beginner who has never performed a butterfly stroke cannot translate a verbal description of the arm recovery into co-ordinated physical movement without also seeing it. Verbal guidance requires the performer to have a mental model they can attach the words to; beginners lack this model. Long verbal explanations can overload a beginner’s attention, particularly in a complex sport like cricket or gymnastics where many technical details need to be processed simultaneously.

Verbal guidance relies on the performer having a mental model to attach the words to. When a coach says “rotate your hips earlier in the swing”, an experienced golfer immediately knows what this means and can make the physical adjustment. A beginner who has never performed a golf swing has no stored movement programme, so the instruction is essentially meaningless until they have experienced the physical sensation. This is why coaches typically combine verbal guidance with a visual demonstration, particularly with beginners. The combination — see it, hear it, try it — is far more effective than words alone.

3. Manual Guidance

Manual guidance involves the coach physically moving or supporting the performer. A gymnastics coach manually guiding a child’s arms through a cartwheel, a swimming instructor supporting a learner’s hips at the water surface, or a judo coach positioning a student’s stance are all forms of manual guidance. By moving the performer through the correct pattern, the coach gives them a kinaesthetic “feel” for the movement that words and demonstrations cannot fully convey.

Advantages of manual guidance: Provides the performer with the physical sensation of the correct movement, giving kinaesthetic feedback that purely visual or verbal guidance cannot. Particularly valuable for beginners learning dangerous or technically complex skills — the coach’s hands provide both safety and a movement template. Builds the learner’s sense of what “correct” feels like, which helps them self-correct in later attempts.

Disadvantages of manual guidance: The main risk is dependency — the performer becomes reliant on the physical support and cannot replicate the movement without it. Coaches must therefore phase out manual guidance progressively as the learner internalises the pattern. For elite performers, manual guidance is rarely appropriate as it interrupts the automatic motor programme they have spent years developing. Physical contact requires the performer’s consent and may not be appropriate in all contexts.

4. Mechanical Guidance

Mechanical guidance uses physical aids to support or constrain the movement. Swimming armbands, a harness and pulley system for a diver practising a new somersault, a resistance band guiding arm position in a backstroke drill, or a bowling target lane for cricket batsmen are all mechanical guidance devices. Like manual guidance, mechanical guidance provides the performer with a physical sensation of the correct movement and removes the risk of injury during the learning phase.

Advantages of mechanical guidance: Allows the performer to experience the physical sensation of the correct movement while removing danger. Particularly useful when the skill carries a high injury risk if performed incorrectly — a diver learning a new somersault in a safety harness can feel the correct rotation without the risk of a head or neck injury. Builds confidence in a dangerous skill. Can be used without a coach present once set up.

Disadvantages of mechanical guidance: Dependency is a significant risk, mirroring the problem with manual guidance. A swimmer who relies on armbands does not develop genuine water confidence or correct buoyancy control. Mechanical aids slightly alter the feel of the movement — a diver in a harness does not experience the full physical sensation of an unsupported rotation, so adjustment is still needed when the aid is removed. Aids can be expensive and are not always available in community sport settings. Elite performers rarely require mechanical guidance for their primary sport skill.

Key Fact

For beginners: visual guidance (demonstration gives a mental blueprint) and manual guidance (physical support gives the kinaesthetic feel) are most effective. For elite performers: visual guidance (video analysis) and verbal guidance (precise technical cues) are most appropriate — elites have existing movement patterns in memory and can translate a single cue into a physical adjustment without needing full demonstrations or physical support.

Key Fact

Over-reliance on manual or mechanical guidance creates dependency: the performer can only replicate the skill with physical support. Coaches should phase out these aids progressively — the goal is independent skill execution. Safety is the primary reason for using manual and mechanical guidance with beginners, not permanent support.

The type of skill also influences guidance choice. Closed skills (gymnastic routines, diving, swimming stroke) are performed in predictable, stable environments and involve repetitive, pre-planned movement programmes. Manual and mechanical guidance are very effective for closed skills because the movement pattern can be physically rehearsed without the complication of an unpredictable environment. Open skills (football passing, rugby tackling) take place in changing environments and require adaptive decision-making. Visual guidance (demonstrations of decision scenarios, video analysis of match positioning) and verbal guidance (calling tactical cues during open drills) are better suited to open skill development. Mechanical guidance cannot replicate the unpredictability of an open-skill environment, which limits its usefulness for open-skill training.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On 6-mark analyse questions about guidance, the most effective structure is: name the guidance type → explain its key feature → link it specifically to either a beginner or elite performer with a sporting example → justify why it suits that performer level. A common error is saying “visual guidance is good for beginners” without explaining why (beginners have no stored movement pattern to draw on, so seeing the skill demonstrated provides the mental blueprint they need). On the 8-mark evaluate question, always address both benefits and limitations of each guidance type, applying your points to the scenario. Read the scenario carefully — if the question specifies a beginner, the examiner wants to see why, for example, verbal guidance alone would be insufficient. OCR’s levels-based mark scheme rewards range of guidance types discussed, balance (benefits and limitations), and consistent sporting application throughout.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The four guidance types are: visual (seeing — demonstrations or video), verbal (hearing — spoken or written cues), manual (physical assistance from a coach) and mechanical (equipment or aids constraining or supporting movement).
  • Beginners benefit most from visual and manual guidance — they need a model to copy and a physical feel for the movement. Over-reliance on manual and mechanical guidance creates dependency and should be phased out progressively as competence develops.
  • Elite performers benefit most from precise verbal guidance and video-based visual analysis, because they can translate specific technical cues into physical adjustments using their well-developed long-term movement memory.

lessons.title: Types of Feedback in Sport
lessons.description: Intrinsic, extrinsic, knowledge of performance, knowledge of results, positive and negative feedback.
lessons.content_html:
Why Feedback Matters in Sport

Every time a gymnast sticks a landing, a coach calls a correction, or a tennis player hears the crowd react to a shot, information is flowing. That information — feedback — is at the heart of how athletes learn, refine skills and progress. Without it, performers would repeat errors indefinitely. With the right type of feedback, delivered at the right moment, improvement accelerates.

The OCR specification organises feedback into three overlapping categories: its emotional tone (positive or negative), its source (intrinsic or extrinsic), and what it tells you (knowledge of results or knowledge of performance). A single piece of feedback can belong to more than one category simultaneously — for instance, a coach saying “that was an excellent drive, but your follow-through was cut short” is extrinsic, partly positive, partly negative, and contains knowledge of performance.

Positive and Negative Feedback

Positive feedback confirms that an action was performed correctly. It reinforces the movement pattern in the performer’s memory, making it more likely to be repeated. A coach saying “great shoulder rotation on that serve” or a crowd applauding a clean strike are both positive feedback. For beginners especially, positive feedback is powerful — it builds confidence and keeps motivation high at a stage when errors are frequent and self-belief is fragile.

Negative feedback highlights what went wrong and, ideally, what should be done differently. The term “negative” does not mean unkind or demoralising — it simply means the feedback signals a mismatch between what was intended and what was produced. A rugby coach who tells a player “your tackling angle is too narrow, step out wider next time” is giving negative feedback that is precise and constructive. Elite performers often seek and welcome negative feedback because they are confident enough to use it as a tool rather than a threat.

Key Fact

Positive feedback is especially important for beginners because it builds confidence and reinforces correct movements. Negative feedback becomes more valuable for elite performers, who need precise detail on how to refine already high-level technique.

Intrinsic and Extrinsic Feedback

Intrinsic feedback (also called internal feedback) comes from the performer’s own body. It travels through sensory channels: proprioception (the sense of where your limbs are in space), vision, touch and hearing. A gymnast knows her balance beam routine felt fluent because her proprioceptive system reports smooth weight transfer and correctly timed muscle contractions. A cricketer senses from the impact vibration through the bat handle whether the ball was struck from the middle of the bat. Intrinsic feedback is instantaneous and continuous — it arrives during and immediately after every movement.

For intrinsic feedback to be useful, the performer must have the experience and body awareness to interpret the sensations correctly. Beginners often struggle to do this — they may feel that a movement went well when it did not, because they lack the kinaesthetic reference point of what “correct” feels like. Elite athletes, by contrast, are highly attuned to intrinsic feedback: Mo Farah described being able to sense the precise moment his running economy started to drop in the final 200 m of a 5,000 m race.

Extrinsic feedback (external feedback) originates outside the performer. Sources include coaches and teachers, peers, video analysis, heart rate monitors, scoreboards and the crowd. Because it comes from outside, extrinsic feedback can fill the gaps that intrinsic feedback misses — for example, a sprinter cannot feel the exact angle of her block start, but her coach can see it on a camera and give precise corrections.

A common error is assuming that because intrinsic feedback is immediate, it must be accurate. Beginners lack the kinaesthetic memory to judge “correct” feeling — a novice swimmer may feel that her arm entry is clean when it is actually crossed over the midline. This is precisely why extrinsic feedback from a coach or video is so critical in early learning: it provides a reliable external reference point until the performer builds a more accurate internal model. Do not confuse “immediate” with “accurate” in your exam answers.

Knowledge of Results and Knowledge of Performance

Knowledge of results (KR) tells the performer what the outcome was: the shot went wide, the javelin landed at 42 metres, the race was completed in 13.8 seconds. It is always extrinsic because the result is separate from the movement itself. KR is easy to understand and motivating — seeing a time improve from 14.2 s to 13.8 s gives a clear signal that training is working — but it tells the performer nothing about why the result was what it was, or how to change it.

Knowledge of performance (KP) focuses on the quality of the movement: the hips rotated too early, the release angle was too flat, the elbow position was correct. KP is richer than KR and more directly actionable because it tells the performer what to change. A coach watching a discus thrower and saying “your pivot foot twisted before your non-throwing arm swept across — you lost rotation” is giving knowledge of performance. Elite performers typically benefit more from KP because their outcomes are already competitive and fine technical detail is what separates them from rivals.

Key Fact

Knowledge of results (KR) = the outcome (time, score, distance). Knowledge of performance (KP) = the quality of the technique. KR motivates; KP teaches. Elite performers need both, but KP is the more powerful learning tool.

Choosing the Right Feedback for the Performer

The effectiveness of feedback depends on the performer’s stage of learning. Beginners benefit most from positive feedback (to build confidence), extrinsic feedback (because intrinsic awareness is unreliable), and knowledge of results (which is simple to understand). Overloading a beginner with detailed KP can cause confusion and undermine motivation.

Elite performers, on the other hand, respond best to specific negative and positive feedback on technique (KP), as well as their own well-developed intrinsic feedback. They also benefit from extrinsic sources such as video analysis and data from performance monitoring equipment. The key principle is that feedback should always be actionable — vague comments such as “try harder” or “that was good” without further detail have little learning value regardless of the performer’s level.

Students sometimes think the six feedback types are mutually exclusive — that a piece of feedback can only be one thing. In fact, they always combine. A coach telling a hockey player “your penalty flick was right on target — perfect height, but your run-up was too slow” is simultaneously: extrinsic (from the coach), positive (right on target, perfect height), negative (run-up too slow), and knowledge of performance (it addresses technique, not just the outcome). Practise identifying all applicable types from a single feedback statement in your exam answers — each type identified and explained earns separate marks.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On a 2 marks — Define question, you need a precise one-sentence definition. “Positive feedback is good feedback” earns nothing — you must specify what it does (reinforces correct actions) and when it is most effective (for beginners). For a 4 marks — Explain question, give the definition (1 mark), explain the mechanism (1 mark), add the sporting example (1 mark), then link to the level of performer (1 mark). A very common error on feedback questions is confusing intrinsic/extrinsic (the source) with positive/negative (the tone) — these are separate dimensions and should never be swapped. On an 8 marks — Evaluate question about feedback types, avoid writing only about one performer level. The mark scheme rewards a balanced argument: positive feedback for beginners (with reasons), knowledge of performance for elite performers (with reasons), then a reasoned conclusion about which approach is more effective and why.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Feedback has three dimensions: emotional tone (positive or negative), source (intrinsic or extrinsic), and what it tells you (knowledge of results or knowledge of performance). These categories overlap — a single piece of feedback can fit all three simultaneously.
  • Beginners benefit most from positive, extrinsic feedback and simple knowledge of results; elite performers gain more from specific, technique-focused knowledge of performance and their own well-developed intrinsic feedback.
  • Feedback must be actionable to have learning value — vague praise or criticism does not help performers identify what to change or repeat.

lessons.title: Health, Fitness and Wellbeing
lessons.description: Defining health, fitness and wellbeing and the physical, emotional and social benefits of sport.
lessons.content_html:
Defining Health, Fitness and Wellbeing

Three terms sit at the heart of this topic, and OCR expects you to define each precisely. Health is defined by the World Health Organisation as a state of complete physical, mental and social wellbeing — not merely the absence of disease. A person can be healthy without being a high-level athlete, and an athlete can be medically fit yet psychologically or socially struggling. True health is multi-dimensional.

Fitness refers to the ability to meet the physical demands placed upon the body. A marathon runner is fit for her event; a weightlifter is fit for his. Fitness is always relative to the activity — there is no single universal measure. Wellbeing is the broader sense of being in a positive state — feeling satisfied, purposeful and capable across physical, emotional and social dimensions. Physical activity contributes to all three simultaneously, which is why it is one of the most powerful public health tools available.

Key Fact

OCR requires three distinct definitions: health (complete physical, mental and social wellbeing), fitness (ability to meet the demands of the environment) and wellbeing (positive state across physical, emotional and social dimensions). These are not the same thing — you can be fit but unhealthy, or healthy but not at peak fitness.

Physical Benefits of Participation

Regular physical activity produces a wide range of physical health benefits, many of which directly reduce the risk of the most serious long-term diseases. The OCR specification names seven physical outcomes you must know: reduced risk of coronary heart disease (CHD), improved blood pressure control, increased bone density, reduced risk of obesity, reduced risk of Type 2 diabetes, improved posture, and improved overall fitness.

Coronary heart disease: regular aerobic exercise strengthens the heart muscle, increases stroke volume and improves the elasticity of blood vessels. These adaptations reduce the risk of fatty deposits narrowing the coronary arteries. Over a lifetime of regular activity, the risk of a fatal heart attack is significantly reduced. Dame Sarah Storey, for example, has maintained exceptional cardiovascular health through decades of competitive cycling.

Blood pressure: regular activity keeps blood vessel walls flexible and reduces the resting demands on the heart, helping to maintain blood pressure within a healthy range. Hypertension (high blood pressure) is a major risk factor for stroke and kidney disease, and inactivity is one of its primary causes.

Bone density and posture: weight-bearing exercise — running, gymnastics, team sport — stimulates bone remodelling, maintaining or increasing bone density and reducing the long-term risk of osteoporosis. Good muscular strength and balanced muscle development also support healthy posture, reducing the back pain and joint problems that arise from prolonged sitting or muscular imbalance.

Obesity and Type 2 diabetes: regular exercise burns energy and maintains muscle mass, supporting a healthy body composition and preventing obesity. Physical activity also improves the body’s sensitivity to insulin, meaning blood glucose is regulated more efficiently. Both obesity and Type 2 diabetes are strongly associated with inactivity, and both significantly increase the risk of further cardiovascular and metabolic disease.

Emotional Benefits of Participation

OCR specifically names three emotional benefits: improved self-esteem and confidence, better stress management, and positive body image. These are not optional extras — they carry equal mark-scheme weight to physical benefits in extended-response questions.

Self-esteem and confidence: achieving a personal best, mastering a new skill or winning a competition builds self-esteem. The process of setting a goal, training towards it and succeeding creates a sense of personal effectiveness that transfers into other areas of life. For young people in particular, sporting achievement can become a foundation for confidence in school, relationships and future careers.

Stress management: moderate to vigorous exercise triggers the release of serotonin, a neurotransmitter linked to feelings of calm and happiness, and endorphins, natural pain-relieving chemicals that produce a sense of euphoria. The neurological effect is a measurable reduction in perceived stress and anxiety. Regular exercisers show lower baseline cortisol (the stress hormone) levels and a faster physiological return to calm after stressful events.

Body image: physical activity improves body composition and physical capability, both of which contribute to a more positive body image. This is particularly significant for adolescents, for whom body image is a major determinant of self-worth. Sport provides an experience of the body as something capable and powerful, rather than something purely aesthetic.

Stress is the body’s physiological response to a perceived threat or challenge. When stressed, the hypothalamus activates the adrenal glands to release adrenaline and cortisol. These hormones raise heart rate, blood pressure and blood glucose, preparing the body for action. Chronically elevated stress hormones damage the cardiovascular system, suppress immunity and impair sleep.

Exercise provides the body with a legitimate outlet for this physiological state. A run or a football training session allows the body to use the elevated heart rate and glucose productively. After exercise, serotonin and endorphin levels remain elevated for several hours, creating a period of improved mood and reduced anxiety. Over time, regular exercisers show lower baseline cortisol levels. This is why physical activity is increasingly recommended by mental health professionals as a first-line intervention for mild anxiety.

Social Benefits of Participation

OCR names three social benefits: the development of friendship, a sense of belonging to a group, and the reduction of loneliness. These are genuine, evidenced outcomes of regular participation and are especially important for specific age groups.

Team sport and group exercise demand cooperation and communication. Playing in a netball team, a rowing eight or a football squad requires trust, shared responsibility and collective problem-solving. These interpersonal skills transfer directly to workplaces and communities. For children and young people, regular team sport is one of the most effective ways of developing the social skills that underpin healthy adult relationships.

Participation also creates structured social contexts where friendships form more easily. For individuals who are isolated — whether through disability, life transitions or mental health difficulties — joining a sports club can directly address loneliness. The shared purpose and regular contact of a club or team provide exactly the conditions in which new social bonds develop. For older adults, group exercise classes and walking clubs perform the same function, reducing social isolation and the health consequences that accompany it.

OCR explicitly requires you to “apply the above to different age groups”. This means you should be able to discuss how the benefits differ across children, young people, adults and older adults. For children: skill development, bone density, socialisation through team sport, building lifelong habits. For young people: stress management, body image, self-esteem, social belonging. For adults: CHD prevention, stress relief, maintaining healthy weight, social connection. For older adults: bone density maintenance (reducing osteoporosis risk), managing Type 2 diabetes, reducing loneliness, maintaining mobility and posture. In an extended-response question, referencing a specific age group with an example will push an answer from Secure to Mastering.

Key Fact

OCR’s named physical benefits: reduced CHD, improved blood pressure, increased bone density, reduced obesity risk, reduced Type 2 diabetes risk, improved posture, improved fitness. Emotional benefits: self-esteem/confidence, stress management, positive body image. Social benefits: friendship, belonging to a group, reduced loneliness. All 13 outcomes are examinable.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The most common error on wellbeing extended-response questions is writing only about physical benefits. OCR’s mark scheme distributes points across all three dimensions: physical, emotional and social. Structure your answer in three clear sections and aim for at least two named benefits per dimension. For a 3 marks — Calculate from Data question, always show your working, state the unit, and make a clear interpretive statement — quoting figures without explaining what they show earns only partial credit. On an 8 marks — Evaluate, OCR rewards (a) range of points across all three dimensions, (b) a balanced argument (sport improves wellbeing and the argument that these improvements vary by age group or type of activity), and (c) consistent sporting application. Use a “For X… However Y…” structure with a named sporting example anchored to each side.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Physical activity produces seven named physical health benefits (including CHD prevention, improved bone density, reduced obesity and Type 2 diabetes risk) alongside three emotional benefits (self-esteem, stress management, body image) and three social benefits (friendship, belonging, reduced loneliness).
  • The three dimensions are interconnected: improved physical health supports positive emotional wellbeing, and social participation through sport reinforces both. Addressing all three in exam answers is essential for higher marks.
  • OCR expects you to apply benefits to specific age groups: bone density matters most for children and older adults; stress management is especially relevant for young people; loneliness reduction is particularly significant for older adults.

lessons.title: Sedentary Lifestyle and Consequences
lessons.description: What a sedentary lifestyle is and how inactivity contributes to obesity, CHD, diabetes and poor wellbeing.
lessons.content_html:
What Is a Sedentary Lifestyle?

A sedentary lifestyle is one defined by prolonged physical inactivity. The word “sedentary” comes from the Latin for “sitting”, and that is its defining feature: large portions of waking hours spent sitting or lying down, with minimal structured exercise. Modern technology has made sedentary living increasingly easy — screen-based entertainment, desk-based work and motorised transport can combine to mean that some individuals complete fewer than 2,000 steps a day. The Health Survey for England consistently shows that a significant proportion of adults fail to meet the recommended 150 minutes of moderate activity per week.

The consequences of a sedentary lifestyle are cumulative and wide-ranging. They span physical health (weight gain, disease), emotional health (poor self-esteem) and social health (loneliness). Understanding these consequences as distinct but interconnected categories is important for exam answers and for appreciating why public health campaigns consistently promote active living.

Key Fact

The six key consequences of a sedentary lifestyle on OCR are: obesity, coronary heart disease (CHD), Type 2 diabetes, hypertension, low self-esteem and loneliness. Each one is examinable as a named consequence, and each should be linked to the mechanism by which inactivity causes it.

Physical Consequences of Inactivity

Obesity: without regular physical activity to burn energy, intake consistently exceeds expenditure and the surplus is stored as body fat. Obesity is defined as excess body fat accumulation sufficient to adversely affect health, typically measured by a BMI over 30. Once present, obesity creates a secondary cascade — it limits mobility, which makes further activity harder, reinforcing the sedentary cycle. Unused saturated fat also accumulates in blood vessel walls, contributing to atherosclerosis (artery narrowing).

Coronary heart disease: a sedentary heart is a weaker, less efficient heart. Without the regular challenge of aerobic exercise, the heart muscle does not strengthen and blood vessels lose elasticity. Fatty deposits accumulate in the coronary arteries, progressively narrowing them. If a coronary artery becomes blocked, the result is a heart attack. Physical inactivity is one of the most modifiable risk factors for CHD.

Hypertension: Hypertension (high blood pressure) is strongly associated with physical inactivity. Without regular exercise to strengthen blood vessel walls and maintain their flexibility, resting blood pressure tends to rise. Hypertension damages arterial walls over time, increasing the risk of stroke, kidney disease and further cardiovascular damage.

Type 2 diabetes: physical inactivity reduces the body’s sensitivity to insulin, the hormone that regulates blood glucose. When cells become resistant to insulin, blood glucose remains persistently elevated. Over time this develops into Type 2 diabetes, which carries serious long-term complications including nerve damage, vision problems and cardiovascular disease. Regular exercise improves insulin sensitivity, which is why physical activity is a primary recommendation for preventing and managing Type 2 diabetes.

The physical consequences of a sedentary lifestyle do not operate independently — they form a self-reinforcing cascade. Inactivity leads to weight gain and obesity. Obesity increases blood pressure (hypertension) and worsens insulin resistance (Type 2 diabetes). Hypertension and fatty deposits from obesity narrow the coronary arteries, raising CHD risk. Meanwhile, low fitness levels make exercise feel difficult, reinforcing the sedentary behaviour. Understanding this cascade as an interconnected chain — rather than a list of separate conditions — will help you write more analytical extended-response answers.

Emotional and Social Consequences of Inactivity

Low self-esteem: physical inactivity is associated with weight gain, reduced self-efficacy and a more negative physical self-image. Self-esteem — one’s sense of personal worth — is strongly linked to how people perceive their own bodies and capabilities. Individuals who are inactive may lose confidence in physical settings, withdraw from sport and social activity, and develop a negative cycle in which low confidence further reduces the motivation to become active.

Loneliness: physical activity is a major vehicle for social interaction. Team sport, gym classes, recreational clubs and even informal park runs all provide structured opportunities for social contact. A sedentary individual who is no longer engaging in these activities loses a significant source of social connection. Over time, reduced social contact leads to loneliness, which itself has documented negative effects on both mental and physical health — including increased blood pressure, poorer immune function and a higher risk of depression.

A sedentary lifestyle is not inevitable — it is a behavioural pattern shaped by environment, habit and access. Strategies to combat it include: increasing active transport (walking or cycling to school/work), taking regular breaks from desk-based work to stand or move, joining a local sports club, and using activity-tracking technology to set daily step or movement goals. At a societal level, urban planning (safe cycle lanes, green spaces, accessible sports facilities) and workplace wellness programmes directly address the structural drivers of inactivity. OCR may ask you to apply these strategies in context, linking them to the named consequences they prevent.

Key Fact

For exam answers: every named consequence must be linked to its mechanism. Obesity = energy surplus stored as fat. CHD = arterial narrowing from fat accumulation + weakened heart. Hypertension = loss of arterial elasticity and flexibility. Type 2 diabetes = reduced insulin sensitivity. Low self-esteem = negative body image + withdrawal from activity. Loneliness = reduced social contact from inactivity.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On a 2 marks — Define question for “sedentary lifestyle”, one mark is for the basic definition (extended inactivity / largely sitting), and the second is for a specific example or consequence. “A lifestyle where someone does very little exercise” earns 1 mark; adding “such as spending most waking hours at a screen or desk” earns the second. For a 6 marks — Analyse question on sedentary lifestyle consequences, structure your answer by grouping consequences: start with the physical chain (obesity → CHD → hypertension → Type 2 diabetes), then address emotional (self-esteem) and social (loneliness) consequences separately. Each point must include a mechanism, not just a label. For 3 marks — Calculate from Data or 4 marks — Interpret Data, quote specific figures, show your working, state the unit and then make an explicit inference about the implications for health.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A sedentary lifestyle is characterised by prolonged physical inactivity and causes six named consequences on OCR: obesity, coronary heart disease, hypertension, Type 2 diabetes, low self-esteem and loneliness — spanning physical, emotional and social health.
  • The physical consequences form an interconnected cascade: inactivity leads to obesity, which drives up blood pressure and worsens insulin resistance, together raising the risk of CHD and Type 2 diabetes.
  • The emotional and social consequences reinforce the physical ones: low self-esteem reduces motivation to exercise, and loneliness removes the social drivers that keep many people active, sustaining the sedentary cycle.

lessons.title: Diet, Nutrition and Hydration
lessons.description: Components of a balanced diet, the role of macronutrients and the effect of hydration on performance.
lessons.content_html:
Energy Use in Sport and Exercise

Everything the body does — breathing, thinking, sprinting, lifting — requires energy. That energy comes entirely from the food we eat and is derived from a combination of macronutrients. The amount of energy an individual needs depends on several factors: age, gender, body size and, critically for athletes, the amount and intensity of exercise performed. A 16-year-old county-level swimmer training twice a day will have far greater energy needs than a sedentary adult of the same age and size.

OCR focuses on energy use — understanding how the body uses different nutrients as fuel — rather than precise calorie calculations. The key principle is matching food intake to energy demand: an athlete needs to consume enough of the right foods to fuel training, support recovery and maintain a healthy body composition.

Key Fact

An individual’s daily energy requirement is affected by age, gender, body size and energy expenditure (exercise levels). Athletes and highly active individuals need significantly more energy than sedentary people of the same age and gender. Energy balance — intake matching expenditure — is the key principle for maintaining a healthy body composition.

The Balanced Diet: Seven Components

A balanced diet does not mean eating equal amounts of everything. It means eating the right proportions of different food types to supply the body with all the nutrients it needs. OCR requires knowledge of seven components: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, minerals, vitamins, fibre and water. No single food provides every nutrient — variety is essential. The approximate proportions for macronutrients in a balanced diet are: 55–60% carbohydrate, 25–30% fat, and 15–20% protein.

Macronutrients: Carbohydrate, Fat and Protein

Carbohydrate is the primary and preferred fuel for all types of exercise, regardless of intensity. Whether a performer is jogging at a comfortable pace or sprinting at maximum effort, carbohydrates are the first fuel the body calls upon. They are broken down into glucose, which is either used immediately or stored as glycogen in the muscles and liver for use during exercise. Elite distance runners and cyclists often practise ‘glycogen loading’ — consuming carbohydrate-rich meals in the days before an event to maximise glycogen stores. Dina Asher-Smith, for example, works carefully with nutritionists to ensure her glycogen stores are fully loaded before major championships.

Fat provides more energy per gram than carbohydrate, but it can only be used efficiently as a fuel source at low intensity — for example, during a slow, steady-state walk or easy cycle ride. When exercise intensity increases, the body switches back to carbohydrate because fat metabolism is too slow to meet the energy demand. Fat also has important non-energy roles: it insulates the body, protects vital organs, and acts as a carrier for fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K).

Protein is not a primary energy source. Its main role is the growth and repair of muscle tissue — essential after heavy training when muscle fibres have been broken down by the work they have done. Adam Peaty follows a protein-rich recovery plan after intense pool sessions to support muscle repair and adaptation. Consuming insufficient protein slows recovery and limits the muscle adaptations that training is designed to produce.

Key Fact

A balanced diet is approximately 55–60% carbohydrate (main energy source), 25–30% fat (energy at low intensity; insulation; vitamin carrier), 15–20% protein (growth and repair). Carbohydrate is the body’s preferred fuel at all exercise intensities.

Micronutrients: Vitamins, Minerals and Fibre

Vitamins and minerals do not supply energy directly, but they are essential for the efficient working of all body systems. Vitamins support processes from immune function (vitamin C) to bone metabolism (vitamin D); minerals such as calcium are vital for bone density and muscle contraction, while iron is essential for oxygen transport in the blood via haemoglobin. A diet lacking variety will typically be deficient in vitamins and minerals even if its total energy looks adequate.

Fibre is the indigestible component of plant-based foods — found in fruit, vegetables, wholegrain cereals and legumes. Its primary role is to support healthy digestion by adding bulk to stools and maintaining regular bowel function. Fibre also helps regulate blood glucose levels after meals by slowing the absorption of sugar, which is particularly important for athletes trying to maintain stable energy levels across a training day.

OCR does not require you to name specific vitamin or mineral requirements for athletes. However, the general principle is that athletes engaged in heavy training have higher micronutrient needs because they use more energy, lose more minerals through sweat (especially sodium and potassium) and undergo greater physiological stress. Female athletes in endurance sport are particularly vulnerable to iron deficiency because of the combined losses through menstruation and high training volume. A varied, whole-food diet is the recommended way to meet these increased needs — supplementation is not always necessary or effective.

Hydration and the Consequences of Dehydration

Water is the medium in which almost every chemical reaction in the body takes place. Maintaining water balance is critical to performance. Even a 1–2% reduction in body mass through fluid loss can begin to impair sporting performance. Dehydration occurs when the body loses more fluid than it takes in. During intense exercise in warm conditions — such as a cross-country race or a summer football tournament — sweat rates can be high, meaning fluid must be replaced regularly to maintain both performance and safety.

Effects of Dehydration on the Body and Performance

Dehydration triggers a series of interconnected physiological problems. As fluid is lost, blood plasma volume falls and the blood becomes thicker. This increase in blood viscosity means the heart must work harder to push blood around the circulatory system, driving up heart rate. Delivery of oxygen and nutrients to muscles slows, accelerating fatigue. In warm conditions, the body’s ability to shed heat through blood vessels near the skin is also compromised, raising core body temperature and increasing the risk of overheating.

Beyond the cardiovascular effects, dehydration also affects the nervous system. Reaction time slows and decision-making deteriorates — a basketball player who is even mildly dehydrated may make slower, poorer decisions on court. Muscle function degrades too: dehydrated muscles fatigue more rapidly and are more prone to cramping, because the electrolyte balance (sodium, potassium) that enables muscle contraction is disrupted. Staying hydrated before, during and after exercise is therefore a non-negotiable aspect of sports performance for athletes at any level.

A common misconception is that hydration simply means “drink lots.” The key concept is fluid balance — replacing what is lost through sweat, breathing and urine, not overloading the body with fluid. For exam answers, the reward is for understanding the cascade of effects from dehydration: blood plasma falls → blood viscosity rises → heart rate increases → oxygen delivery slows → muscles fatigue and cramp → reaction time slows → decision-making deteriorates. Practise writing that chain in order, anchored to a sporting context.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On a 3 marks — Calculate from Data question involving nutrition percentages, always show your working, state the unit (%), and present a clear final answer. For example: if asked what percentage of a 3,000 kcal diet should come from protein at the minimum recommended level, the working is 3,000 × 0.15 = 450 kcal. Missing the unit drops a mark. On a 4 marks — Interpret Data question, quoting figures without explaining what they mean earns partial credit only. Always make a comparison, quote at least one figure, then explain the sporting implication. For an 8 marks — Evaluate question about diet and performance, avoid listing nutrients in isolation. Structure your answer around the demands of the specific sport or performer, then link each nutrient to how it meets those demands — or what happens if it is insufficient. A counter-argument (e.g. too much protein without adequate carbohydrate will not improve performance) earns marks in the upper bands.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A balanced diet contains seven components: carbohydrates (55–60%, main energy source), fats (25–30%, low-intensity energy + insulation), protein (15–20%, muscle growth and repair), plus vitamins, minerals, fibre and water. Carbohydrate is the body’s preferred fuel at all exercise intensities; glycogen stores are the athlete’s key energy reserve.
  • Vitamins and minerals maintain efficient body system function; fibre supports digestion and stable blood glucose; water is the medium for all physiological processes.
  • Dehydration increases blood viscosity, raises heart rate, causes overheating, slows reactions, impairs decision-making and leads to muscle fatigue and cramping — all of which degrade sporting performance at any level.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'balanced diet'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the basic definition: a diet containing the correct proportions of all the nutrients the body needs. 1 mark for development: states the seven components (carbohydrates, protein, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre, water); or states the approximate proportions (55-60% carbohydrate, 25-30% fat, 15-20% protein); or gives a sporting example (e.g. an endurance runner needs a higher carbohydrate proportion than a sedentary individual to fuel long training runs).

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows the daily macronutrient breakdown of two club-level swimmers during a training week.

Swimmer | Total daily energy | % from carbohydrate | % from protein | % from fat
Aisha | 2,800 kcal | 57% | 18% | 25%
Ben | 2,800 kcal | 44% | 22% | 34%

Using the data, identify which swimmer has a macronutrient balance within the recommended ranges for a balanced diet, and calculate the amount of energy Ben obtains from fat each day.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying Aisha as within balanced-diet ranges: carbohydrate 57% (within 55-60%), protein 18% (within 15-20%), fat 25% (within 25-30%). Ben is outside range (44% carbohydrate is below 55% minimum; 34% fat exceeds 30% maximum). 1 mark for correct calculation: 2,800 x 0.34 = 952 kcal from fat. 1 mark for stating the unit (kcal) and confirming Ben's fat intake exceeds the recommended maximum of 30%.

practice_questions.text:
Table 2 shows heart rate data for two players during the final 20 minutes of a 90-minute football match played in hot conditions. Player A drank water at half-time; Player B drank nothing during the match.

Time | Player A heart rate (bpm) | Player B heart rate (bpm)
70 min | 148 | 163
80 min | 151 | 172
90 min | 149 | 181

Interpret what the data shows about the effect of dehydration on Player B's heart rate, and explain why this change occurred.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that Player B's heart rate is consistently higher than Player A's across all three time points (163 vs 148 at 70 min, rising to 181 vs 149 at 90 min). 1 mark for quoting specific figures to support the comparison. 1 mark for linking the rising heart rate to dehydration increasing blood viscosity (thicker blood). 1 mark for explaining the mechanism: the heart must beat faster to maintain adequate blood flow to working muscles when blood is thicker, accelerating fatigue and performance decline in the final stages of the match.

practice_questions.text: Explain how an adequate intake of carbohydrate and protein would help a county-level rower prepare for and recover from a five-day intensive training camp.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining carbohydrate's role in preparation: stored as glycogen in muscles and liver, used as the primary fuel during high-intensity rowing training; adequate carbohydrate ensures glycogen stores are full before each session. 1 mark for explaining carbohydrate's role during the camp: replenishing glycogen stores after each session maintains energy availability for subsequent sessions across the five days. 1 mark for explaining protein's role in recovery: muscle fibres are broken down during intense rowing training; protein provides the amino acids needed for repair and adaptation (hypertrophy). 1 mark for a link to performance: insufficient protein slows repair, leaving the rower fatigued and limiting the training adaptations the camp is designed to produce.

practice_questions.text: A 17-year-old club-level long-distance runner is preparing for her first half-marathon. Her coach has recommended she follow a carefully planned diet for the six weeks before the race. Evaluate the extent to which carbohydrate, protein and hydration are each important to her preparation and race performance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): presents a balanced evaluation of all three nutritional factors applied specifically to a long-distance runner preparing for a half-marathon; argues the case for carbohydrate (primary fuel, glycogen loading in final days, sustained energy during the 90+ minute race); argues the case for protein (muscle repair across the six-week training block, limiting injury and supporting adaptation); argues the case for hydration (dehydration raises heart rate and blood viscosity, slows reactions, causes muscle cramps, particularly dangerous in a long-duration event); evaluates relative importance with justification (e.g. carbohydrate is arguably most critical on race day because glycogen depletion is the primary cause of 'hitting the wall'; however, without adequate protein across the training block there would be insufficient muscle adaptation to compete); at least one developed counter-argument; sporting application sustained throughout.

Secure (5-6 marks): covers all three factors with explanation; links to the long-distance running context mostly present; some evaluation of relative importance; conclusion present.

Developing (3-4 marks): covers two factors accurately; links to the athlete context limited; limited evaluation; conclusion may be present but not fully justified.

Emerging (1-2 marks): one or two basic accurate points about nutrition or hydration with little sporting application or evaluation.

glossary_terms.definition: A diet that contains the correct proportions of all essential nutrients the body needs for health, growth and energy.
The body's main and preferred energy source for exercise, broken down into glucose and stored as glycogen in muscle and liver.
The stored form of glucose in the muscles and liver, used as a fuel source during exercise.
A macronutrient used primarily for the growth and repair of muscle tissue, not as a major energy source during exercise.
Organic compounds needed in small amounts to support immune function, bone health, energy metabolism and other essential body processes.
Inorganic elements needed in small amounts for processes such as bone formation (calcium), oxygen transport (iron) and fluid balance (sodium).
The indigestible part of plant-based foods that supports healthy digestion and helps regulate blood glucose and cholesterol levels.
A state of insufficient water in the body, caused when fluid lost through sweat, respiration and urine exceeds fluid taken in.
The thickness or resistance to flow of blood; dehydration increases blood viscosity, making it harder for the heart to pump blood to working muscles.
